scenes.title: The Final 2 Hours and 40 Minutes
scenes.narration: At two twenty in the morning, Titanic disappeared beneath the North Atlantic. Two hours and forty minutes earlier, her lights were still burning. How did a ship built to survive a collision run out of time?

scenes.title: A ship built on land
scenes.narration: Before there was a disaster, there was a shipyard in Belfast. Harland and Wolff built Titanic for the White Star Line. In the photograph, the hull rises over the men and machines that made it.

scenes.title: Eight hundred and eighty-three feet
scenes.narration: Titanic stretched nearly eight hundred and eighty-three feet from end to end. Steam drove three propellers beneath the stern. The funnels and rows of deck windows made the scale of the ship visible from the quay.
scenes.visualDescription: Wide maritime reconstruction. Ocean liner carries the scene: eight hundred and eighty-three feet.

scenes.title: The floating hotel
scenes.narration: White Star sold the crossing as an experience in itself. First class had a gymnasium on the boat deck, elaborate public rooms and private suites. Elsewhere on the same ship, passengers travelled with very different expectations.

scenes.title: The promise of subdivision
scenes.narration: Below the public decks, bulkheads divided the hull into watertight compartments. Closing doors could isolate flooded sections. Several forward compartments flooding at once could defeat the design.

scenes.title: Leaving Southampton
scenes.narration: On the tenth of April, nineteen twelve, Titanic left Southampton for New York. This photograph shows the ship at Southampton on the day she sailed. Once clear of the port, she turned towards the English Channel.

scenes.narration: The first stop was Cherbourg, on the French coast. Next came Queenstown, in Ireland, where more passengers boarded. From there, the voyage opened out into the Atlantic, with New York on the far shore.

scenes.title: A crossing of many lives
scenes.narration: Some passengers could afford the best rooms on the ship. Others were travelling in third class, carrying what they could towards new lives. Behind the passenger lists were families, people travelling alone and people crossing for work.
scenes.visualDescription: Archival photograph. Mounted archive print carries the scene: a crossing of many lives.

scenes.title: The work beneath the decks
scenes.narration: The ship depended on hundreds of crew. Stewards kept the passenger decks running. In the stokeholds, firemen fed coal into the boilers. Above them, officers and lookouts worked in watches as the liner crossed the ocean.

scenes.title: Into the open Atlantic
scenes.narration: Once Ireland fell astern, the passengers had open water ahead of them. For days the ship held a westward course. On Sunday, the fourteenth of April, wireless messages began to describe ice lying across that passage.

scenes.title: Ice on the route
scenes.narration: Ships reported icebergs and fields of ice. The messages gave positions, and several reached Titanic's bridge. Together, the warnings placed ice in the ocean she was approaching.

scenes.title: A busy wireless room
scenes.narration: Titanic's wireless operators also handled passengers' messages. A particularly detailed warning from Mesaba never reached the bridge. Late that night, Californian reported she had stopped in ice. By then, the ships were working on different priorities.

scenes.title: A dark sea
scenes.narration: The night was clear, with no moon to light the horizon. The sea was unusually smooth. There was little swell to break against the base of an iceberg and make it easier for a lookout to distinguish.

scenes.title: Ice directly ahead
scenes.narration: From the crow's nest, the lookouts saw ice ahead. The warning went to the bridge, and the ship began to turn. The interval between sighting the iceberg and reaching it was measured in seconds.

scenes.title: A glancing blow
scenes.narration: At about eleven forty at night, the iceberg scraped along the starboard side. The contact was brief. Below the waterline, damage extended far enough along the forward hull to let water into several compartments.

scenes.chapter: 04 / The Final Two Hours and Forty Minutes
scenes.title: The first minutes
scenes.narration: Water poured into forward spaces, including a boiler room. Men below deck could see what the impact had done long before many people above them understood. Watertight doors closed, but the flooding already extended across multiple sections.

scenes.title: As the bow settles
scenes.narration: With the bow settling, water could rise above the top of a bulkhead and pour into the next section. Each flooded space pulled the ship lower. The pumps could not keep pace with that progression.

scenes.chapter: 04 / The Final Two Hours and Forty Minutes
scenes.title: A call in the night
scenes.narration: After midnight, the wireless operators sent distress calls and gave a position. They used the older signal, C Q D, and also sent S O S. A ship that could hear them still had to reach them.

scenes.chapter: 04 / The Final Two Hours and Forty Minutes
scenes.title: A ship answers
scenes.narration: One of the ships that answered was Carpathia. Her captain, Arthur Rostron, turned towards the distress position and ordered full speed. There was ice between the two ships, and the distance could not be crossed quickly enough.

scenes.chapter: 04 / The Final Two Hours and Forty Minutes
scenes.title: Too few places
scenes.narration: Titanic carried twenty boats, including four collapsibles. On paper, they had room for fewer than twelve hundred people. More than two thousand were aboard. Even a perfectly organised launch could never have carried everyone away.

scenes.chapter: 04 / The Final Two Hours and Forty Minutes
scenes.title: Two twenty
scenes.narration: At about two twenty, Titanic sank. The wreck would later show that the ship had broken apart. Two hours and forty minutes had passed since contact with the ice. In the darkness, those in the water needed immediate help.

scenes.title: After the lights
scenes.narration: The people in the boats could hear those in the water. In the near freezing sea, exposure could kill quickly. For the people already afloat, darkness and the fear of swamping complicated any decision to row back.

scenes.narration: Fifth Officer Harold Lowe took a boat back to look for survivors. This photograph was taken later, after daylight, as his boat towed a collapsible towards Carpathia. It records the rescue in the small craft themselves.

scenes.title: Carpathia among the ice
scenes.narration: At about four ten in the morning, Carpathia picked up the first boat. Ice still surrounded the rescue ship. Its crew recovered boats scattered over several miles until about eight.

scenes.title: The survivors
scenes.narration: About seven hundred people survived. Around fifteen hundred died. The historical counts differ, but the imbalance is unmistakable. For those brought aboard Carpathia, survival came with the uncertainty of who else had made it out.

scenes.narration: Carpathia arrived in New York on the eighteenth of April. By then, newspapers had carried estimates that changed as information reached shore. Families waiting for names still had to discover whether an absence was permanent.

scenes.title: The search below
scenes.narration: For more than seventy years the wreck's position remained unknown. In nineteen eighty-five, a French and American expedition searched the sea floor. The teams used sonar and then towed cameras, looking for a trail of debris.

scenes.title: An unmistakable shape
scenes.narration: Early on the first of September, the cameras passed over a boiler. Its shape told the team what they had found. Titanic lay southeast of Newfoundland, nearly three thousand eight hundred metres beneath the surface.

scenes.title: Questions on shore
scenes.narration: The British and American investigations gathered testimony about the warnings, the ship's speed, the boats and the rescue. Their records preserve accounts that sometimes disagree. What they made public was the chain of decisions that preceded the loss.

scenes.title: Safety of life at sea
scenes.narration: In nineteen fourteen, a new international convention addressed safety of life at sea. The disaster sharpened attention to lifeboat capacity, wireless watches and ice patrols. The lessons could now reach ships beyond the company that had lost Titanic.

scenes.title: A line marked by experience
scenes.narration: The International Ice Patrol gave ships a way to track the moving danger that Titanic had met in darkness. Reporting positions became part of a shared system. Ships could use those reports to plan safer routes.

scenes.title: What remains
scenes.narration: Titanic is still remembered for what people made possible in Belfast. The lasting measure of the ship, though, is human. More than two thousand people went to sea together. For most of them, that crossing never ended.
